segments.text: Hello friends. This is Brian Johnson, author of zeroism. A few times in my life, I've read books that have changed the way I understand my life and reality. I hope this is one for you. Enjoy. Episode 1 A people's history of zeroism.

Hello everyone. My name is Zero. In this video, I'm going to walk you through zeroism, which is my personal philosophy for the future of being human. It's going to be a tour of the past, the future, and the interior of the human mind as it contemplates an existence so different, so unimaginable that it drives many to an existential crisis.

But first, I need to set the record straight. Yes, in 2022, I did receive 1 L of my 17-year-old son's plasma. However, unlike what was reported in the media, my son is kept in a room that is 8 by 8, not 10 by 10.

Also, I have high expectations of my son. Specifically, he must do the following things. First, do well in school. Second, complete his household chores. Third, give me 1 L of his plasma. And fourth, clean his room.

Now, I'm just kidding about cleaning his room. You might have just heard of me recently, maybe this year. Maybe you heard about some rich guy doing crazy things and trying to live forever. Or maybe the YouTube algorithm brought you here.

Isn't it funny how quickly we gave decision-making authority to AI about where our minds should go next? Huh. More on that later. Or maybe you're here because you read Ashley Vance's profile on me in Bloomberg, How to be 18 years old again for only $2 million a year.

I was born 46 years ago, but my left ear is 64, my heart is 37, and my cardiovascular capacity is in the top 1.5% of 18-year-olds. After working on the scientific frontiers of anti-aging for 3 years, I'm not really sure how old I am anymore.

My health endeavor Blueprint has been full of surprises. For example, discovering that my left ear has a biological age of 64. I am basically deaf in my left ear from 4,000 Hz to 12,000 Hz. I had no idea. As a kid, I shot a lot of guns, and I listened to a lot of loud music. And we never wore hearing protection. It turns out, hearing protection is really important.

It was also surprising that after sharing for free everything I was learning about my health and wellness, the global response was a tsunami of hate. I became detested from far-reaching corners of the globe. People called me a narcissist, a vampire, an elf, Patrick Bateman, Dorian Gray. Surely, I must be an Illuminati lizard person. Shh, that's true.
No part of me was off-limits to ridicule. I was accused of being too pale, too skinny, too vain, too muscular, too reptilian, too idiotic, too too. Whatever that even means.
Wild, what is happening? People confidently stated that Blueprint must exist because I am miserable and trapped in a cage of my own making. That in its implementation, I am missing the point of life.

Why extend life? What's the point? They psychoanalyzed me, diagnosing me with a crippling fear of death, and more personality disorders than there are people. They suggested I am a fool on a vain quest for immortality. But for the record, I have never said I am pursuing immortality. I have said we no longer know how long and how well we can live.

They said I was yet another arbitrary person in yet another arbitrary time on another arbitrary continent on a failed quest for the Holy Grail. He'll do anything to avoid therapy. Just live life. We're all going to die, so what does it matter? Were the common refrains.
The reactions reminded me of patterns I've seen in the biographies I've read. In every era, 99% of those who lived lived in the past, living by the ideas, norms, and traditions of dead people.

The future in every era had always arrived. They just hadn't seen it yet. Or they hadn't recognized it as the future, or they had seen it and then outright rejected it. The same is true for us right now. We are no different. The future is always here. It's just hiding in plain sight.
It's a game of who can spot it. My project Blueprint proposed that a radically different future is here, and true to form, it's hiding in plain sight. I'm going to tell you right now, here it is.

Death might no longer be inevitable. When I said this, armies of death defenders pulled out their swords and charged me. I live near Hollywood, and no joke, movie studios came to me asking if they could learn the details of my life to inspire their next major villain.

I admit, at first, the vitriol confused me. But soon, I realized that most of it was just group therapy. It is a response from a society addicted to addiction. I believe the animosity was all just a confession of helplessness.

Amid the hate storm, no one seemed to understand what I was really proposing, because if they did, they might have truly lost their minds. All right, before we get into the details, let's start with some context, like the whole context.

For 13.8 billion years or so, who knows, the number is always changing, there has been a universe. Earth has been around for 4.5 billion years or so. We were single cells for most of that. Fast forward a bit, and boom, Homo sapiens. Different. We're so so different.

We're intelligent. We think. We think about thinking. We lived what maybe a couple decades at most back then. We laughed. We loved. We reproduced. We died. Just like all other life. Then, after a couple hundred thousand years, our species suddenly levels up.

And massively. We get fire, language, agriculture, cities, writing, industry, electricity, nuclear, solar, internet. And then, AI. It took almost 13.8 billion years, but finally, intelligence made more intelligence. Finally, at long last, intelligence has made a different kind of intelligence that evolution couldn't create on its own.

It's different, yes, but is it better? What would that even mean? We are, in fact, baby steps away from creating superintelligence, which very well might be the most extraordinary event in the history of the universe.

Life was special. Life is special. But this, this is different. Superintelligence will rewrite reality. It will pop, one after another, the bubbles we live in, revealing to us dimensions and realities far beyond our imagination and comprehension.

This is why I started zeroism. Over the past few years, after hearing me explore and build the tenets and pillars of zeroism in private, my friends and family nicknamed me Zero, and it stuck. Zero sits at the origin, at the 0 0 coordinate of the biggest revolutions in history.

It is from this position that we are stepping into what could surely be the most magnificent existence in this part of the galaxy. But before we get there, I must tell you about this Brian Johnson guy and how he died to make room for Zero, as I think we may have more in common than you think.

Episode 2 Firing Evening Brian. I'm going to get personal here for a minute. In my 20s and 30s, life got pretty dark. I was raising three kids, wrestling a challenging personal relationship, starting and building multiple companies, and dealing with chronic depression.

I was trying to leave my born-into religion, and it all started to stack up. It was a bonfire. At night, after fighting the day's battles, and then feeding, bathing, telling stories to, and putting the kids to bed, I often thought of one of Mother Nature's best defense mechanisms, perfected by the opossum.

I just wanted to fall to the ground and play dead. Maybe, I thought, when it got really bad, I don't even have to play anymore. Maybe I didn't have to pretend anymore. Despite how I felt, at around 7:00 p.m. each night, I would have the most comforting, optimistic thoughts.

The brownies. Just eat the brownies. The kitchen isn't far. You deserve it. It was a rough day. All that stress burned so many calories, thousands. You read that somewhere, right? Just one will make it all go away. Now, in case you're wondering, that's evening Brian talking. He was a pretty big personality in my life. He made all the decisions back then.

He wanted everything now without the burden of accountability. For years, morning Brian promised that today was a new day. He wouldn't fall prey to the old bad habits. Dad Brian swore he'd be the exemplar father figure he'd always aspired to become.

Then 7:00 p.m. would come and evening Brian would push all other Brians aside and do as he pleased. Evening Brian is not a bad person. In fact, I deeply empathize with him. He's carrying the heavy burdens of all other Brians. He was low on willpower and discipline, and he just wanted the pain to stop.

One day, as the brownies called from the I took a quick stock of myself. I had gained 50 lb, about the size of a Siberian husky. I carried that canine size fat around with me every day. My pants were so tight I had to leave the top unbuttoned.

I was disgusted with myself, and I knew my pattern of hopeful thinking. The Brian, I know what you're thinking. We said tonight would be the last night, but you know what? One more night and tomorrow everything changes. Tomorrow the new awesome merges. Tomorrow everything we want is going to come to fruition. Just tonight, one last time.

I realized in that moment that I had more neurons than anything else in my life. And when those neurons turned on me, I didn't stand a chance. As I began to slip into submission, I jokingly muttered, "Evening Brian, you make my life miserable. You're fired." No, don't do it.

For some reason, acknowledging evening Brian as a distinct version of me to be reckoned with changed something inside of me. Separating my various selves from their behaviors was empowering. I am not the behavior. I am somewhere else.

And I prevailed. I didn't eat the brownies. This small win ushered in a wave of relief. Maybe, I thought, I wasn't trapped forever. I began to understand that there were parts of myself that were unique, each with their own motivations and proclivities. I spent the night thinking about technology that could commune with my various selves, hidden throughout the kingdom of my conscious and unconscious mind.

There's morning Brian, after exercise Brian, work Brian, dad Brian, storytelling Brian, playful Brian, and evening Brian among many others. Each version of myself had a distinct biochemical configuration, states of sad and playful, stressed and angry.

They created predictable patterns of thought, emotions, and behaviors. For example, stressed-out Brian was approximately 100 times more likely to down a whole bag of potato chips than morning Brian. Nobody eats ice cream when they wake up.
Okay, maybe some of you do. Why then, right before bed? Who's really in charge here? I've learned a few lessons building multiple technology and science companies that I think map to this situation.

In technology, version one gives way to version two, which then launches version three. The valuable moves forward. The rest disappears. The key to building any advanced technology is trusting in the process where systematic and methodical improvements create compounded gains.

This is the fastest way to advance anything. Why couldn't I apply this to my mind, my body, my health? All day I labored to make abstract technology better, but while at home, I got worse. I got too little sleep, ate too much unhealthy food, and didn't exercise nearly enough.

I had completely abandoned my personal rate of improvement for the sake of technological progress. I was a martyr for technological advance. But what if I could improve myself at the speed that technology improves? What if we all could? What if decay and decline were not inevitable?

In the 1990s, this would have been ridiculous to suggest. Not anymore. With AI, it is now impossible to predict how well and how long we may live. The night I fired evening Brian, my sleep didn't feel dramatic for the first time in years. It was rejuvenating.

The next day, I was flying to a meeting. I had just gotten my pilot's license. As I journeyed to my destination, my gaze was fixed on the airplane's attitude indicator. My hand gripped the controls as my co-pilot and I steadied the plane at 10,000 ft.

Flying is a never-ending activity of keeping the airplane in optimal position. I noticed a directional drift, so I corrected ever so slightly left, then down, then a tiny bit right. At the same time, I became lost in thought about work, all the fires that needed putting out. My mind wandered. I wondered how much better could I perform if I wasn't weighed down by poor sleep and declining health.

I knew my life was not only stalled, but in a tailspin. If I didn't do something soon, I would freefall straight to the ground. After a few more minutes at the airplane's manual controls, I ceded authority to the engineering automation of autopilot.

I ceded authority to an intelligent system of software and hardware that ingested information from a suite of airplane sensors to make real-time flight decisions. Autopilot freed me to tend to other important flight tasks.

The airplane sat up straight with perfect posture. It pegged the altitude with steadiness, with greater precision than I could with my own abilities. The airplane's instant alignment triggered memories from my flight training in conditions of total blackout. When you learn to fly, you're tested by flying blind to any outside visual reference.

In these moments, your instruments are your only source of truth. Relying solely on intuition in these crucial moments can be dangerous, fatal in fact. Without visual reference points, our body's internal sense of orientation often misleads us. The conscious mind tricks you into believing and seeing things that are not accurate.

To simulate blackout conditions during pilot training, you're asked to wear a hood. It's terrifying at first. You can only see the instrument panels while you're flying. You have no outside reference. So, using your instruments only, you have to safely get the airplane a few hundred feet above the runway and ready to land.

You must master relying upon instruments and trust them with your life. That day, my pilot training collided with my ideas around health and wellness. I wondered, could I build an autopilot for myself, one that would augment my natural abilities?

But what should I call it? My autonomous self. I wondered if an automated system for health, body, and mind could produce compounded gains in me as fast as we see in technological progress. After thinking this through, I was exhilarated when I landed.
Blueprint. I would call it Blueprint. Episode three. What is Blueprint? What single thing can any individual do to maximally increase the probability that humans thrive beyond what we can imagine?

Blueprint's singular objective is to try and hitch a ride into the future by answering this question today. There are three main ideas. Number one, Blueprint. Blueprint is an algorithm that takes better care of me than I can care for myself.

We humans struggle to act in our best interests. We reliably do unhealthy things that accelerate decay, disability, disease, and death, both to ourselves and to our planet. We will look both ways before crossing the street to avoid getting hit by a car, but we will do so while smoking a cigarette.

Every day, we do things that accelerate aging. And while we may think we can stop those things anytime we want, we are powerless to stop them all. Don't believe me? Try stopping all of your self-destructive behaviors. These include eating too much food or junk food, not exercising, smoking, excessive drinking, drugs, staying up past our bedtimes, pornography, excessive social media, and dozens more.

All of these things shorten our lives. All of them make life less enjoyable in the long run. They are payday loans, and the interest is taken from the well-being, happiness, and health of future you. It's not that we want to do bad things.

Okay, yes, we do. Bad things are easy, and good things are hard. To protect ourselves from the raw reality that we are powerless to stop these behaviors, we create pretty stories to justify them. Live a little. We're all going to die anyway.

We are masters at hiding the truth we don't want to see. Blueprint plays a new game called don't die. We in fact play it every day right now. We wear seat belts, we change the batteries in our smoke alarms, and throw out moldy food. Blueprint is don't die expert mode.

This is how I personally play the game don't die. My team and I gather hundreds of biomarkers from my body. This allows my heart, lungs, liver, and 70 other organs to speak for themselves. No more rumors, no more guesswork.

After evaluating hundreds of scientific papers, we then create a health protocol. This algorithm determines what and when I eat, when I go to bed, and so forth. My mind does not have the authority to order from a menu, eat a gallon of ice cream because it's night time, or peruse the pantry because I'm bored. My body's organs and biological processes oversee the whole thing, not my mind.

Sounds dystopic, right? This isn't the future you imagined? Just wait, it gets worse. Number two, the autonomous self. The goal of Blueprint is the autonomous self, where each of us improves at the speed of science and technology.

We are accustomed to our technology getting reliably better. Every year, we get new versions of almost everything. Meanwhile, every day we humans reliably get one day closer to death. Your autonomous self reverses this trend by building upon the foundation of Blueprint to interconnect your well-being and personal growth with the progress of science and technology.

Number three, zeroism. Zeroism is the underlying philosophy of Blueprint and the autonomous self. You can think of zeroism as a version of future literacy, a mindset and toolkit to navigate a rapidly changing and completely unknown future.

Let's put future literacy in context. In 1820, only 12% of the world's population could read and write. Imagine what our daily lives would look like right now if we hadn't achieved an 86% basic literacy over the past two centuries.

We'd probably be significantly less prosperous, healthy, and interesting. Historically, future literacy was not imminently needed. Things changed slowly over the course of generations. Knowing seasonal weather patterns was good enough for most people.

Today, there are tectonic, technological, and cultural shifts that happen on the time scales of weeks, months, and years. The pace of change will continue to accelerate. We are accustomed to thinking about human evolution on the time scale of tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of years, not in single lifetimes. But that's where we are now.

We need to be alert to the changes in store for individuals and humanity to triage the right path forward. Ultimately, this is a question of survival. Personally, after observing my own thoughts and behavior for 46 years, I do not trust my conscious mind. Not in a pantry full of junk food, not with my best long-term interests, not in explaining away my irrational behaviors.

I do not think that humanity, as we are configured today as a society, can cooperate well enough and fast enough to avoid catastrophic outcomes. I think we need to hand over the reins of power. Humanity has reached its cognitive and attentional limits in managing a complex, ultra-interconnected world.

Zeroism is a way to understand, think, and behave in a rapidly changing future, a way to anticipate and prepare for the unknown. Intelligence has been what we know. Zeroism is the intelligence of not knowing, embracing what we do not know, what we cannot see, and acting courageously nonetheless.

Throughout history, the number and concept of zero revolutionized math and physics, art, philosophy, and religion. Our modern society depends on the power of zero, enabling computers, gaming, social media, GPS, and medical technology.

Some of history's most monumental breakthroughs are, as I like to call them, zero discoveries. For example, Einstein's theory of relativity, identifying microscopic germs as the culprit of infections, and the vanishing point in early Renaissance art that bridged the gap between 2D and the perception of 3D space.

Each of these discoveries previously existed. They had just remained invisible until someone identified them. Zeroism captures this fundamental shift from status quo preservation and rule following of knowns to not knowing, exploring, and adapting.

In the past, discoveries of zero happened every few decades or centuries, popping our bubbles and revealing new dimensions that were previously unknown. For example, that the Earth was not the center of the universe. A few decades or even a century was enough time for society to reconfigure and update its beliefs, technology, and culture.

Zero discoveries are now happening at a much faster pace. That is because AI is a zero manufacturer. Insights generated by AI will introduce reality-bending zeros and demand that we quicken our adaptation.

So there you have it, three ideas. Blueprint. We humans are going to be run by algorithms because they are superior to us. Some of us will kick and scream the whole way, but this change is inevitable.

Once we are through this transition, we will forget that we ever resisted the upgrade in the first place. In fact, we will pity our former selves. Autonomous self. We will begin improving ourselves at the speed of science and technology because we can.

Zeroism. In a rapidly changing future, our best attribute is learning a new form of intelligence, which is not knowing, also known as future literacy. Zeroism is a response to the fact that humanity is facing at least three imminent and existential risks. Number one, the risk of an unsustainable biosphere.

Two, misaligned AI. And three, mass destruction via nukes, bio-warfare, societal collapse, etc. We need to choose our path forward. In evaluating these risks, do you think humanity, through nation-states, corporations, ideologies, and individuals, can cooperate and problem-solve on the necessary time scales to avoid an insufferable existence and/or extinction?

I'll pose this question another way. Could it be the case that humanity would be better off rethinking how we make decisions going forward? In the same way that I did with my health, empowering science, data, and an algorithm to care for me better than I can care for myself.

A computational system of intelligence. To help you build intuitions around computational systems, imagine empowering Earth's biosphere to manage its own well-being. We humans are currently in charge of deciding how much pollution and toxicity we generate, and whether the oceans become more acidic, the planet warms, and more life becomes extinct.

If our biosphere were in charge, we'd use the same Blueprint process to fix its problems. Measuring the biosphere via oceans, atmosphere, land, etc. via millions of data points. Following scientific evidence for sustainable conditions, and empowering algorithmic adaptation for Earth's health markers to be achieved.

Our biosphere sets the standards for pollution, toxins, wildlife, and weather. Humanity deals with it and adapts. Said differently, the former me ate whatever he wanted, whenever he wanted it, no matter the damage.

Current me hops into and follows what my body's organs are asking for in order to achieve ideal health. Most of humanity treats planet Earth the same way we treat our bodies, doing pretty much whatever we want, whenever we want, no matter the damage. It's why we're in the tricky predicament of having a rapidly changing and increasingly violent biosphere.

In hearing these ideas, many confidently assert that my motivation for Blueprint is a fear of death. I do not fear death. I sat at its doorstep for a decade alongside chronic depression, desperately wishing I didn't exist.

Had it not been for my three children, I probably would have taken my own life. I know what it's like to be locked into a staring contest with death. I now feel an insatiable love of life deeper than I've ever experienced.

I also know that my future self, perhaps the version that exists when superintelligence has arrived, may understand existence in ways that are inconceivable to me now. Here, right now, wanting life can be hard for so many reasons.

The depths of depression taught me a thing or two about this. I dream of an existence where we all want to keep playing the game of life, even in our darkest moments. For thousands of years, it's been the same story. We're born and then we die in predictable fashion.

Don't die is the ultimate game to play. Existence is the highest virtue. The concept of God is a zero, an idea to explain what we do not and cannot know. We are all zero and our existence could be that which we cannot imagine.

It takes courage to confidently step into the unknown. Right now, in the early 2020s, we can't assume that anything that has been true will continue to be true. Anyone who says otherwise doesn't understand what's really going on.

Baby superintelligence is already here and improving faster than our minds can comprehend. Blueprint is not just for me, it is for everyone. Blueprint is a plan to save ourselves. May we have the courage to believe that right now may be the very beginning.
Episode 4. Zeroism as a belief system. At the age of 34, I sold my payments company, Braintree Venmo, for 800 million in cash, the fulfillment of my life dream.

Instead of it being this unhinged celebratory moment I'd imagined it would be, it was just one more complication to deal with. At the time, my 13-year marriage was unraveling. Our three kids were aged 10 and under and it broke my heart and my brain to imagine that we would now be a split family.

I was wrestling to leave my born into religion. I'd lost my bearings, not knowing anymore what was up or down, what was left or right. To help you better understand this moment, I'll paint the picture for you. When I was 19 years old, I was a Mormon missionary sent to Ecuador.

It was the first time I went outside the rural bubble of Mormon Utah. I had come home only to question the nature of everything I had been taught. It became clear that I'd spent the first 19 years of life comfortably encased within several bubbles, unaware of their limitations and boundaries.

I had been inside belief systems wrapped in belief systems, each shaping my conscious mind. I had grown up in a rural community of 30,000 people. Everyone was Mormon. We all shared a singular understanding of existence.

All I could think about now was, what other bubbles am I in? And if I had learned of these bubbles, how would my understanding of existence change? And if that changed, what different decisions would I make? College was beckoning with its life decisions, major selection, and career path.

I hadn't the faintest idea what I wanted to be or study. The only thing I knew was that my experience in Ecuador had lit a raging fire inside of me. I wanted to spend my life working to improve the lives of others at a societal level.

To do this, I determined that I'd make an enormous amount of money by the age of 30 and then figure out a way to up-level humanity. I told everyone about my master plan. Nothing quite like the arrogance and wonder of a 21-year-old mind.

Now, 10 years later, I found myself encased, feeling paralyzed. Severing my relationship with God and a marriage was a psychological conundrum that was perpetually unsolvable. A decade of chronic depression had not only dropped me into a black hole of hopelessness, but it had me questioning whether I could believe anything I thought or felt.

When I was born into this world, I was told, "Follow these life rules and an omnipotent being will crown you with eternal life." Looking back, how beautifully simple, if only it were true. I am not anti-religion. I am pro-existing and anti-death.

Growing up, I was asked to bet my existence on a hypothesis that is testable only upon death. In any other time during the past few hundred thousand years, it wouldn't have mattered whether someone accepted the gamble or not.
Everyone was guaranteed to die anyways, so why does it matter? But what if? What if? Then I read Zero, a biography of a dangerous idea by Charles Seife. Nothing in my mind has been the same since.

What a surprise it was to learn that the number zero was discovered. Of course it was. I just hadn't thought about it. Like the idea behind every great revolution, the concept of zero wasn't birthed into the world easily. It caused a stir in philosophy, math, ideology, and society before it revolutionized each.

Zeroism is a way of thinking that has helped me in my mental efforts to seek out the undiscovered, what lies beyond the fog. Zeroism digs into what is hidden in plain sight, just as the number zero once was.

Zeroism allows me to reach out and feel the intangible and amorphous, the kinds of ideas that have been transformative to civilizations, heliocentrism, the discovery of germs, and Einstein's special and general theories of relativity. These are all zeros. They were not discovered based upon what we knew, but rather what we didn't know.

Zeroism is a system of thought one level deeper than so-called first principles thinking. If zeroth principle thinking is building blocks, first principle thinking is all about understanding the nature of the building blocks. Many people spend their entire lives as first principle thinkers. There's nothing wrong with this. Some professions demand it.

Consider the fictional Sherlock Holmes. He's a first principle thinker. He believes, according to his famed maxim, that when you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth.
Zeroism invites you to think like Dirk Gently, a different kind of detective conceived of by the sci-fi humorist Douglas Adams. Dirk Gently is a zero detective. The zero detective rules nothing out.

Instead, they begin by wondering if the impossible solution makes more sense. It is a search for the building blocks themselves, not how they work. When someone is thinking from a first principle perspective, they're likely going to start by assuming the fewest number of things within a given time frame.

Zeroism, however, doesn't try to identify or rule out the impossible. It wonders if we might not be seeing the structure of reality immediately in front of us. Zeroism leads us to the possible, not the probable, to the previously undiscovered.

Zeros are game-changers. In a world where we are continuously expanding our spheres of understanding, each zeroth principle insight can potentially unlock a set of more expansive spheres. This is bigger than an exponential effect, a hockey stick curve.
With a zero, the graph is not just exponential, the units change. The graph reorganizes its axes. Dimensions are added to accommodate ideas from another dimension. That's what zeros get you.
Zeroth principle thinking paves the way to explore boundless terrain. We have entered an era that will be defined by an avalanche of zero-like ideas. That is because AI is a zero factory.

Understanding our very existence has become a quest for zeros. Already, we are seeing zeroth principle ideas come to fruition at a faster rate than ever before, which means we're driving into this future with fog in all directions.

Previously, we humans could make reasonable assumptions about what might exist beyond our field of view. Deductive reasoning and a dash of first principle thinking every century or so used to be enough. Not anymore.

Evolving, adapting, and collaborating with AI will require fluency in zeroism. To that end, I've been working on a system for evolving ourselves so that we humans can roll with the changes that AI brings, no matter how the terrain shifts.

The goal is to align ourselves towards harmony instead of our own demise. So, what is the potential payoff? Well, that's a surprise. To begin our journey as zeroists, we can seek to identify the building blocks of intelligence. Our bodies and minds are a fruitful place to begin this exploration.

Episode 5. The First Supper. The ideas around Blueprint and Zeroism challenge the core of our current identities. Many people, upon hearing these ideas for new models of the future, either boomerang some form of hatred or fall into existential despair, unsure how to climb out of the pit dug by their previous selves.

I've seen this happen so many times that I realized I needed to soften the blow, which led me to start hosting Blueprint brunches, which I call the first supper. In a private and comfortable setting, I present the ideas and then create enough space and time for the participants to have multiple existential crises. At the supper's end, the participants rise with a basic level of reconciliation. My favorite follow-up notes to receive are those that explain how the conversation broke their brain in ways they didn't know it could be broken.

And then they add they haven't been able to stop ruminating about the ideas since. I suspect that the more time the idea sits in your mind, the more its inevitability creeps in. It's hard to find arguments supporting the idea that we can remain as we are and survive.

The evolutionary pressure presented by advances in AI, a changing biosphere, and unforeseen and unpredictable future events invite, no, demand that we improve our speed of evolutionary adaptation. First supper guests have included scientists, philosophers, engineers, educators, artists, astronauts, doctors, and entrepreneurs.

Each gathering lasts around two to three hours. The meals all have the same arc. To prepare the group for the provocative nature of the conversation, I provide some thought experiments. I start with a simple question we all supposedly know the answer to.

How many glasses of water should you drink each day? "Eight." Someone always says. "How do you know that?" I ask. "I read it somewhere, or maybe my parents told me. I don't know." This exercise highlights what most of us experience daily across the majority of the decisions we make about health and wellness. Our insides are off-limits. We use hunches, folk remedies, and antidotes.
